splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that carry criminal penalties or sentencing enhancements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should trump deference to agency interpretations in the criminal context. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. This matters because it determines whether ambiguous sentencing guidelines are construed in favor of or against defendants.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions or sentencing enhancements, meaning ambiguity should be resolved in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor) prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing courts to defer to agency interpretations of ambiguous sentencing guidelines even when they expand criminal liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders with significantly higher sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, making conspiracy convictions qualifying predicates for career-offender status.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' meaning conspiracy convictions cannot serve as career-offender predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means 'and' or 'or.' The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits read it conjunctively (defendant must meet all three criteria to be disqualified), while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits read it disjunctively (any one criterion disqualifies). This split directly affects mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenders and creates geographic disparities in criminal sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally scheduled. Some circuits hold the definition broadly encompasses any state law offense, while others require the substance to be controlled under federal law. This affects whether state drug convictions can serve as predicates for significant sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: Broad — includes any state-controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Narrow — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, preventing state convictions for substances not on the federal schedules from serving as sentencing predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's changes to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) stacking) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under the compassionate release statute. The Eighth Circuit held in Crandall that non-retroactive changes cannot contribute to such a finding, while other circuits have permitted consideration of such changes, either alone or in combination with other factors. This split affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences under outdated mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the initial Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held that it belongs to the debtor. This matters significantly for debtors whose property values increase during bankruptcy proceedings.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), means that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the structure of the Bankruptcy Code, post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors, not the estate, consistent with the statute's purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether they may also use civil rights statutes like Bivens actions.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoners challenging not just the fact or duration of confinement but also the conditions and terms of confinement, including BOP decisions about prerelease custody under the First Step Act. This affects thousands of federal prisoners' ability to seek judicial review of BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus may be used to challenge conditions of confinement and BOP decisions about terms of custody, including prerelease custody determinations under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement — as distinct from challenges to the fact or duration of confinement — should be brought through civil rights actions rather than habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to promoting the defendant's reentry into the community.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit under United States v. Lewis allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at an extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should focus on the defendant's breach of the court's trust and reentry, not punishment for the underlying conduct. This affects sentencing for hundreds of supervised release revocations annually.

positions.label: Punishment for the violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions at revocation hearings, in addition to considering reentry and public safety.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should focus on reentry, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentences is to sanction the breach of the court's trust and promote reentry, not to punish for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the time limit for appealing a Hyde Amendment order (for attorney's fees in a criminal case) is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (triggering the 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined what it described as the majority view holding it is a civil matter, but acknowledged a circuit split exists. This affects the ability of acquitted defendants to seek reimbursement of legal fees.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires that actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans be fixed by the end of the prior plan year or may be selected afterward. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for the thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls withdrawal liability amounts.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), giving employers greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may adopt actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how federal courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authority.

positions.label: Fugitive tolling applies to supervised release
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be adjudicated, based on equitable principles and the supervisee's own misconduct.

positions.label: Fugitive tolling does not apply without statutory authorization
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to toll supervised release in the absence of explicit statutory authorization, meaning the term runs even while the supervisee is absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented — when filing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from re-raising claims, creating a stricter gatekeeping requirement beyond what § 2255(h) alone requires. This significantly affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge their convictions collaterally.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically preventing them from re-raising any claim that was presented in a prior collateral attack.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements (newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law) when filing successive motions, and the additional (b)(1) bar does not apply.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. Some circuits grant candidates broad standing based on competitive injury, while others require a more concrete showing of harm. This split affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing based on competitive injury
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for office have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election based on the competitive injury of running under allegedly unlawful rules.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing without concrete harm
positions.summary: Holds that candidates must demonstrate more than a generalized competitive injury to establish Article III standing for pre-election challenges, requiring concrete and particularized harm.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have taken narrower views of what privacy interests qualify for immediate appellate review. This split affects litigants' ability to protect sensitive medical information during litigation.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses are immediately appealable because maintaining medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that warrants immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because privacy interests can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
